dashboard.description: Comprehensive interactive reference and live demonstration of the React & D3.js custom AWS Data Flow Diagram visualizer.

div.h1: AWS Security Data Flow Diagram (DFD) Visualizer
div.p: Welcome to the AWS-DFD-Visualizer, a React-based custom visualization for Splunk built to render complex multi-cloud relationships (supporting **AWS**, **Microsoft Azure**, and **Google Cloud Platform**) as dynamic, interactive Data Flow Diagrams. This app is architected with DoD Impact Level 5 (IL5) environments, Risk Management Framework (RMF) audits, and Zero-Trust architecture (ZTA) in mind. Section 1.3 keeps three lists apart: allowed flows, planned changes, and the actual rows. The app does not include an allow list.

div.p: The visualizer reads standard tabular results from your SPL query. You should format your query using | table or | project to yield the following columns:

table.style: color: #dcdcdc; width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid #444; margin-top: 10px; margin-bottom: 20px;

td.style: padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #444; font-weight: bold; color: #FF9900;

tr.td: The source node resourceId or full AWS ARN. ARNs are normalized internally for safe D3 selections.

td.style: padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #444; font-weight: bold; color: #879196;

tr.td: The destination node resourceId or ARN. If left empty, an isolated node is drawn without connections.
AWS resource type, used to resolve service-specific architectural icons automatically.

Human-readable label shown inside the node card. To ensure readability by leadership, use coalesced fields and never output raw IDs unless for Tier 3 troubleshooting (e.g., eval node_label = coalesce(Name, Role, resourceId)).
Relationship descriptor text overlaying the link curve. Prohibited from being empty ("ghost arrows") in Tier 1 & 2 views. Use "Contained In" for hierarchical/containment links.
Pillar/security zone name. Nodes of the same group are drawn inside curved, shaded convex hulls.
Configuration status. Statuses like ResourceDeleted render cards with reduced opacity and dashed borders.
Configuration capture timestamp. Older snapshots trigger stale-node fade-out animations.

panel.title: 1.2. Integrated Data Source Targeting & SPL Best Practices

div.p: When query-generating data from live AWS Config JSON tables or building mock datasets, adhere strictly to the following ingestion best practices:

ul.li: JSON Targeting: Base queries on sourcetype="aws:config" or equivalent JSON formats. Utilize spath to extract fields cleanly.
Memory-Safe Relationship Extraction: Always append a limit when expanding relationship arrays (e.g. | mvexpand rels limit=1000) to prevent high-volume workloads from hitting Splunk memory caps.

Schema Field Retention: Ensure extended attributes (subnetId, vpcId, and securityGroups) are explicitly returned in your terminal | table command, even if not represented as nodes. These fields are mandatory to drive active drilldowns and concentric compliance rings.

Mandatory Group Boundaries: Nesting structures correctly requires formatting the group field inline: | eval group = case(isnotnull(vpcId) AND isnotnull(subnetId), vpcId . "/" . subnetId, isnotnull(vpcId), vpcId, 1=1, "GLOBAL_ROOT").
JSON Escaping inside SPL: When hardcoding mock nodes (e.g. via | makeresults), all quote characters inside the JSON strings (such as securityGroups) MUST be escaped with a backslash: \".

Tabular Schema Padding: If using append combinations, initialize empty attributes (e.g. subnetId="" vpcId="" securityGroups="") on non-infrastructure layers to prevent schema mismatch rendering failures.

Audience-Centric Labels: Never output raw AWS IDs in the node_label unless explicitly required for a Tier 3 Troubleshooting view. Always use the coalesce pattern to ensure readability by leadership: | eval node_label = coalesce(Name, Role, resourceId).

Explicit Edge Typing: Unlabeled links ("ghost arrows") are prohibited in Tier 1 and Tier 2 views. Always populate edge_label. If the link represents structure or containment (e.g., EC2 instance inside a Subnet), use: | eval edge_label = "Contained In".

panel.title: 1.3. Allowed, planned, and actual — column contract and source recipes

div.p: The diagram draws the rows your search returns. It does not ship an allow list, and it does not allow or deny packets. Keep three lists, and keep them apart:

ul.li: Allowed (<your_allowed_flows>) is what is approved. A flow may run because the authorization says so.
Planned (<your_planned_flows>) is a change inside a plan. It is not yet allowed. Leave it out of the allowed lookup until a person approves it.
Actual is the live search. It is the evidence. Indicators of compromise join onto these rows only.

div.p: OK means the actual row is in the allowed lookup. violation means an actual row is not allowed, an allowed row is missing from the actual search, or an actual row matched an indicator. A planned row that is not yet actual stays planned and is not a violation. A person decides whether a violation may be added to the allowed lookup. The firewall, security group, or Kubernetes network policy is what permits or drops the traffic. This visualization does not call the Governance Policy Inquiry Service. That service allows or denies agent actions.

Put protocol and port in edge_label (for example tcp/443). Put the service name in node_label. The canvas reads those fields today. Always set plane to one of Identity_Plane, Policy_Plane, Control_Plane, or Data_Plane. Collapse repeats with | stats so the result stays under the 5,000-row stop. Replace every <your_*> placeholder with your index or lookup.

ul.li: from, to — required endpoints.
node_label — service name.
edge_label — protocol and port.
group — VPC, subnet, network security group, or Kubernetes namespace.
vpcId — cloud network id when you have one. Leave it empty for on-prem Kubernetes and put the namespace in group.
plane — source or isolated-node band. Kubernetes control-plane components are not the diagram's NIST bands. If plane is empty, a label containing api_server is classified as Data_Plane.
dest_plane — destination band on a hop row. Joined hops set this so the source node is not pinned to the destination plane.
status — OK, violation, or planned, using the rule above. In zero-trust layout the hop paints: red, green, or amber. SSH/22 on a violated node is an extra highlight, not the only red path.

div.p: This canvas does not join Allowed, Planned, and Actual. Feed already-joined rows, or run a customer SPL recipe below. This app does not call the Kubernetes API or GPIS and does not hold a kubeconfig.

Copy reconciliation-rows.csv from ai-agent-governance-framework scripts/join-state.py into this app's lookups. A dogfood copy ships as reconciliation-rows.csv. It is a sample hop table, not an allow list.

div.pre: index=<your_aws_index> sourcetype=<your_vpcflow_or_config_sourcetype> | eval from=coalesce(src_ip, srcaddr, source) | eval to=coalesce(dest_ip, dstaddr, destination) | eval node_label=coalesce(service, from) | eval edge_label=coalesce(protocol, "ip")."/".coalesce(dest_port, dstport, "any") | eval group=coalesce(vpc_id, "unassigned") | eval vpcId=vpc_id | eval plane=case(match(node_label, "(?i)iam|identity"), "Identity_Plane", match(node_label, "(?i)firewall|waf|gateway"), "Control_Plane", true(), "Data_Plane") | stats count by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="actual", ioc_hit=0 | lookup <your_indicator_lookup> dest as to OUTPUT indicator | eval ioc_hit=if(isnotnull(indicator), 1, 0) | append [ | inputlookup <your_allowed_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="allowed", ioc_hit=0 ] | append [ | inputlookup <your_planned_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="planned", ioc_hit=0 ] | stats values(record) as record max(ioc_hit) as ioc_hit by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval has_actual=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^actual$"))) | eval has_allowed=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^allowed$"))) | eval status=case(has_actual>0 AND ioc_hit>0, "violation", has_actual>0 AND has_allowed>0, "OK", has_actual>0, "violation", has_allowed>0, "violation", true(), "planned") | table from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane status

div.pre: index=<your_gcp_index> sourcetype=<your_firewall_or_flow_sourcetype> | eval from=coalesce(src_ip, connection.src_ip) | eval to=coalesce(dest_ip, connection.dest_ip) | eval node_label=coalesce(service, rule_name, from) | eval edge_label=coalesce(protocol, "ip")."/".coalesce(dest_port, "any") | eval group=coalesce(vpc_name, "unassigned") | eval vpcId=vpc_name | eval plane=case(match(node_label, "(?i)iam|identity"), "Identity_Plane", match(node_label, "(?i)firewall|armor|gateway"), "Control_Plane", true(), "Data_Plane") | stats count by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="actual", ioc_hit=0 | lookup <your_indicator_lookup> dest as to OUTPUT indicator | eval ioc_hit=if(isnotnull(indicator), 1, 0) | append [ | inputlookup <your_allowed_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="allowed", ioc_hit=0 ] | append [ | inputlookup <your_planned_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="planned", ioc_hit=0 ] | stats values(record) as record max(ioc_hit) as ioc_hit by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval has_actual=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^actual$"))) | eval has_allowed=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^allowed$"))) | eval status=case(has_actual>0 AND ioc_hit>0, "violation", has_actual>0 AND has_allowed>0, "OK", has_actual>0, "violation", has_allowed>0, "violation", true(), "planned") | table from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane status
div.h3: On-prem Kubernetes — manifests first, then live rows
div.p: Manifests you are still standing up belong in <your_planned_flows> until a person approves them into <your_allowed_flows>. The namespace is the group. This app does not connect to the API server, score the nodes, or enforce Pod Security. After the cluster is online, point the actual search at the flow or audit events you already collect.

Set plane in the search for isolated nodes. For already-joined hop rows use dest_plane (see join-state file above). A common assignment puts kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, and kube-controller-manager on Control_Plane and workloads on Data_Plane. That assignment is yours. Leaving plane empty lets the label api_server fall into Data_Plane.

div.pre: index=<your_k8s_index> sourcetype=<your_flow_or_audit_sourcetype> | eval from=coalesce(src_service, src_ip) | eval to=coalesce(dest_service, dest_ip) | eval node_label=coalesce(k8s_component, service, from) | eval edge_label=coalesce(protocol, "tcp")."/".coalesce(dest_port, "any") | eval group=coalesce(namespace, "unassigned") | eval vpcId="" | eval plane=case(k8s_component IN ("kube-apiserver", "etcd", "kube-scheduler", "kube-controller-manager"), "Control_Plane", true(), "Data_Plane") | stats count by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="actual", ioc_hit=0 | lookup <your_indicator_lookup> dest as to OUTPUT indicator | eval ioc_hit=if(isnotnull(indicator), 1, 0) | append [ | inputlookup <your_allowed_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="allowed", ioc_hit=0 ] | append [ | inputlookup <your_planned_flows> | fields from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval record="planned", ioc_hit=0 ] | stats values(record) as record max(ioc_hit) as ioc_hit by from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane | eval has_actual=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^actual$"))) | eval has_allowed=mvcount(mvfilter(match(record, "^allowed$"))) | eval status=case(has_actual>0 AND ioc_hit>0, "violation", has_actual>0 AND has_allowed>0, "OK", has_actual>0, "violation", has_allowed>0, "violation", true(), "planned") | table from to node_label edge_label group vpcId plane status

panel.title: 2. NIST 800-207 Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) Copy-Paste SPL Scenarios

div.p: You can visualize NIST 800-207 Zero-Trust logical diagrams directly inside Splunk. Copy and paste either of the following standard self-contained SPL searches into a search panel or dashboard to see ZTA rendering in action:
div.h3: Scenario A: Core PDP/PEP Data Access Path
div.p: This scenario models the logical path of a User Subject requesting access to an Enterprise Resource, intercepted by a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), which verifies identity and posture policies with the Policy Decision Point (PE / PA):

pre.style: background-color: #1a222a; color: #5cb85c; padding: 12px; border-radius: 4px; border: 1px solid #333; overflow-x: auto; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.4;

div.h3: Scenario B: Multi-Source PIP Query Engine
div.p: This scenario models the Policy Engine (PE) querying multiple distinct Policy Information Points (PIPs)—such as the User Attribute Registry (IAM), MDM Posture Manager (DEVICE), and Activity Logs audit database (CLOUDTRAIL)—to feed the trust algorithm during an evaluation:

pre.style: background-color: #1a222a; color: #5cb85c; padding: 12px; border-radius: 4px; border: 1px solid #333; overflow-x: auto; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.4;

div.h3: Scenario C: Zero-Trust Multi-Plane Architecture (Identity, Control & Data Planes)
div.p: This scenario models elements across all three Zero-Trust planes (Identity Plane, Control Plane, and Data Plane). It uses modern semantic field aliases (display_name, resource_type, icon_id, plane, group) to automatically position the Corporate IdP and Edge WAF communicating with an App subnet EC2 host in the Data Plane:

pre.style: background-color: #1a222a; color: #5cb85c; padding: 12px; border-radius: 4px; border: 1px solid #333; overflow-x: auto; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.4;

div.pre: | makeresults | eval from="10.0.1.10", to="10.0.2.20", display_name="App subnet host", edge_label="tcp/443", group="Data Plane", plane="Data_Plane", resource_type="AWS::EC2::Instance", icon_id="EC2" | append [| makeresults | eval from="idp.corp", to="10.0.1.10", display_name="IdP", edge_label="OIDC", group="Identity Plane", plane="Identity_Plane", resource_type="AWS::IAM::User", icon_id="IAM"] | append [| makeresults | eval from="waf.edge", to="10.0.1.10", display_name="WAF", edge_label="HTTPS/443", group="Control Plane", plane="Control_Plane", resource_type="AWS::WAFv2::WebACL", icon_id="WAF"] | table from to display_name edge_label group plane resource_type icon_id
div.h3: Scenario D: Live AWS Config Ingestion
div.p: This query handles standard live-data ingestion from `sourcetype="aws:config:json"`. It extracts core resource attributes, formats them to the diagram schema, and uses `mvzip` and `mvexpand` to safely map parent-child relationships and association names without positional shifts:

pre.style: background-color: #1a222a; color: #5cb85c; padding: 12px; border-radius: 4px; border: 1px solid #333; overflow-x: auto; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.4;

div.pre: index=aws sourcetype="aws:config:json" | eval from='configurationItem.resourceId' | eval type='configurationItem.resourceType' | eval node_label=coalesce('configurationItem.resourceName', 'configurationItem.resourceId') | eval group=coalesce('configurationItem.awsRegion', "Global") | eval status='configurationItem.configurationItemStatus' | eval captureTime='configurationItem.configurationItemCaptureTime' | rename configurationItem.relationships{}.resourceId as related_id, configurationItem.relationships{}.relationshipName as relation_name | eval zipped_relations=mvzip(related_id, relation_name, "::") | mvexpand zipped_relations | eval parts=split(zipped_relations, "::") | eval to=mvindex(parts, 0) | eval edge_label=mvindex(parts, 1) | table from to type node_label edge_label group status captureTime
div.h3: Scenario E: Custom Status Palette Integration via Asset Lookup
div.p: This scenario demonstrates how to correlate AWS telemetry data with a local CSV asset inventory (my_asset_inventory_lookup) to dynamically determine configuration status (assigning flags like NonCompliant or EXEMPT) and highlight node borders dynamically using the Custom Status Palette options:

pre.style: background-color: #1a222a; color: #5cb85c; padding: 12px; border-radius: 4px; border: 1px solid #333; overflow-x: auto; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; line-height: 1.4;

div.pre: | makeresults count=1 | eval from="i-0123456789abcdef0", to="i-9876543210fedcba0", type="AWS::EC2::Instance" | append [ | makeresults count=1 | eval from="i-9876543210fedcba0", to="i-unknown-resource", type="AWS::RDS::DBInstance" ] | append [ | makeresults count=1 | eval from="i-11112222333344445", to="i-0123456789abcdef0", type="AWS::EC2::Instance" ] | lookup my_asset_inventory_lookup resourceId as from OUTPUT role as asset_role | lookup my_asset_inventory_lookup resourceId as to OUTPUT role as target_role | eval status = case( isnull(asset_role), "UnregisteredAsset", asset_role="Identity Plane" AND isnull(target_role), "PolicyViolation", true(), "OK" ) | eval node_label = coalesce(asset_role, "Unknown Asset") | table from to type node_label status
div.p: To verify: paste the SPL query above into the visualizer, open the Format Options ➔ General ➔ Custom Status Palette input, and enter: UnregisteredAsset=#EF4444,PolicyViolation=#F59E0B. Unregistered nodes (like the unknown target) will render with red borders, while policy violations will show amber borders.
To establish a stable, aggregated, and compliant static dashboard layout that represents Zero-Trust architecture boundaries, combine the following three mandatory architectural rules:

ul.li: Rule 1: The ROOT_NODE Mathematical Constraint: Hierarchical layouts (non-physics trees) require a single parentless root node to stabilize. The input dataset must inject a virtual parentless node (e.g. ROOT_NODE) for all plane/zone roots to branch from.

Rule 2: The Aggregation & Live-Data Pattern: Instead of listing static templates, use an | inputlookup combined with a | stats count by role | xyseries pattern to dynamically aggregate asset counts into the node labels (e.g., "Policy Engine (4 Active Devices)").

Rule 3: Mandatory Dashboard XML Options: Bypassing Splunk dashboard rendering defects requires explicitly setting and locking the following XML attributes in the dashboard panel configuration:
layoutMode="Hierarchy" - Locks nodes onto static grid positions.
clusterBy="group" - Tells D3 to construct clean, padded rectangular swimlanes wrapping each group.
draggableNodes="false" - Freezes coordinates and disables visual dragging for static briefings.

div.p: Traditional force-graphs frequently suffer from DOM-sync crashes because D3 directly mutates elements managed by React. This visualizer utilizes D3 strictly as a math and physics co-processor to calculate 2D spatial coordinates (handling d3.forceSimulation, collision detection, and zoom matrices), while React retains complete ownership of the DOM (rendering high-fidelity SVG <rect> card elements, images, text, and binding secure events).

When grouping by VPC subnets or security domains (using the group column), the visualizer uses d3.polygonHull combined with a Catmull-Rom closed interpolator to draw shaded convex hulls enclosing the nodes. This allows for immediate visual identification of missing firewalls, insecure trust boundaries, and network segregation breaches in Impact Level 5 (IL5) environments.

In AWS Config relationships, associations are often declared on both ends (e.g. from EC2 pointing to Subnet and vice-versa). The visualizer uses a sorted canonical edge set key ([from, to].sort().join('|')) to automatically prune duplicate connections, preventing D3 forces from double-pulling nodes and collapsing the diagram into visual anomalies.

Traditional D3 force-directed visualizers place a heavy maintenance burden on administrators, who must manually drag cards to organize the layout and save their coordinates. The AWS-DFD-Visualizer completely eliminates this layout persistence overhead via its Pure Deterministic Static Layout Engine. In Blueprint Mode (activated by setting layoutMode="Hierarchy", clusterBy="group", and draggableNodes="false"), new subnets or EC2 scaling groups automatically compute their own structural grid dimensions bottom-up on search refresh. No human dragging, coordinate databases, or manual drag-and-drop maintenance is required.

To prevent visual overlaps with extreme resource labels or compliance badge rings, the visualizer dynamically calculates each node's card bounds using character length metrics (applying a 15% safety buffer for text wrapping). D3 forces (rectCollide and getDynamicLinkDistance) dynamically adapt to these individual node sizes, maintaining a clean physical "Air Gap" (with a maximum 1.5× base gap clamp to retain architectural proximity).
Customize the presentation of your diagram using the visualizer Format menu in the Edit view:

ul.li: Node Placement Mode (display_mode): Switch between Auto (Physics) to allow forces to self-arrange, or Manual (Sticky) to lock nodes where you drop them.
Layout Engine (layoutMode): Choose Force Directed for organic physics layouts or Hierarchy (Tree) to organize nodes as Top-to-Bottom or Left-to-Right BFS trees.
Clustering (clusterBy): Render security envelopes by group by selecting Group.
Draggability and Zoom (draggableNodes / canZoom): Toggles interactivity for static audit exports.
Edge Styling (smoothEdges): Toggle curved SVG paths versus straight vector lines to maximize link legibility.
Multi-Cloud Stencil Set (cspStencilSet): Toggle between Auto (Detect), AWS, Azure, and GCP to control stencil/icon theme parsing.

Governance Terminology (labelIdentityPlane / labelControlPlane / labelDataPlane): Rename the Zero-Trust planes dynamically in the dashboard view. Default labels support emoji prefixes (e.g. ⚙️ Control Plane). Supports dynamic SPL overrides via the zone_name or zone query columns.

Custom Status Palette (statusPalette): Map custom status strings (e.g., NonCompliant, EXEMPT) to hex colors (e.g., #FF6B6B, #4ECB71) via a comma-separated format. User configurations augment built-in compliance highlights (e.g., ResourceDeleted).
